intro: Yungaburra is a small town on the Atherton Tableland in Far North Queensland, inland from Cairns. A kilometre south-west of it, in its own small national park of mabi rainforest, stands the Curtain Fig Tree, a strangler fig whose aerial roots hang in a wall about fifteen metres high. It has drawn visitors since the 1920s and is on the Queensland Heritage Register. A boardwalk from the roadside car park circles it.

trees.story:
The Curtain Fig is a strangler fig, Ficus virens, whose aerial roots drop about 15 metres to the forest floor in a single hanging wall. It stands in Curtain Fig National Park, about a kilometre south-west of Yungaburra on the Atherton Tableland in Queensland, and the Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service puts it at 500 years or more, according to Wikipedia's article, which draws on the Queensland Heritage Register.

The fig began life high in another tree, as these figs do. Its roots strangled the host, which fell against a neighbour at an angle, and the roots that then dropped from the leaning trunk made the curtain. The host has since rotted away. The register gives the fig about 50 metres of height and a trunk circumference of 39 metres.

It has drawn visitors since the 1920s, when hire cars began running day tours across the Tableland, and it was added to the Queensland Heritage Register in 2009.

A reader sent us their photograph from the boardwalk, and it shows the scale. The roots hang in a pale grey sheet from the crown to the ground, and a man at the rail in the foreground is a small dark head below it. A raised timber boardwalk from the roadside car park circles the tree.
trees.how_to_recognise: A wall of pale grey aerial roots hanging about 15 metres from the crown to the forest floor, circled by a raised timber boardwalk with interpretation boards.
